cards.title: Half-snowflake embeddings into Wasserstein p-space
cards.formal: For every fixed real \(p\in(2,\infty)\), does there exist a finite constant \(C_p\ge1\) such that every finite metric space \((X,d)\) admits a map \(F:X\to\mathcal P_p(\mathbb R^3)\) and a scale \(s>0\) satisfying \(s\sqrt{d(x,y)}\le W_p(F(x),F(y))\le C_p s\sqrt{d(x,y)}\) for all \(x,y\in X\)? The constant may depend on p but must be independent of X, its number of points and its distances.
cards.why: Asks how richly a fixed three-dimensional transport space can represent arbitrary finite metric geometry after taking square roots of distances. The proposed exponent would improve the known universality range beyond what follows directly from the transport-cost exponent.
cards.status_note: Read the conference equation, the full journal definitions and Question 23, and the later publisher full-text results on planar snowflake universality. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of bounded-distortion half-snowflake universality for every p>2 in P_p(R³). The extraction’s apparent p before d was the square-root sign, not an exponent or coefficient.

progress.text: The ICALP paper proves 1/p-snowflake universality and states the bounded-distortion half-snowflake conjecture in equation (25).
The full journal treatment retains the conjecture as Question 23, equation (52), while proving sharpness of the known exponent for 1<p≤2.
Later work establishes planar Wasserstein/persistence-diagram relationships for coarse embeddings and 1/p-snowflake universality, a different target.

sentences: The question asks whether every finite metric becomes a bounded-distortion subset of Wasserstein p-space over R³ after taking square roots of its distances.
The exponent p is fixed above two, and the distortion bound must depend only on p.
The known theorem works at snowflake exponent 1/p, which is smaller than one half in this range.
Almost-isometric embeddings and embedding the entire Wasserstein-2 space are separate stronger questions.
The later planar results checked here do not settle this three-dimensional half-snowflake conjecture.

cards.definitions:
A finite metric space consists of a finite set X and a symmetric function d:X×X→[0,∞) with d(x,y)=0 exactly when x=y and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z). Its half-snowflake is the metric space with distance √d(x,y). The square root applies to the original distances, not to the Wasserstein distance or to the dimension. Distances in the base space R³ are the usual Euclidean distances.

The set \(\mathcal P_p(\mathbb R^3)\) consists of Borel probability measures μ on R³ satisfying \(\int\|u\|_2^p\,d\mu(u)<\infty\). A coupling of μ and ν is a probability measure π on R³×R³ with these two marginals. Write Π(μ,ν) for all such couplings. The Wasserstein metric is \(W_p(\mu,\nu)=(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int\|u-v\|_2^p\,d\pi(u,v))^{1/p}\). Thus the transport cost uses the pth power of Euclidean distance and takes a pth root after minimizing. Images may be arbitrary measures of finite pth moment; no support-size, equal-mass, rational-coordinate or computability restriction is imposed.

The two-sided inequality means a bi-Lipschitz embedding of distortion at most C_p after a common rescaling s. It forces F to be injective when X has more than one point. Both F and s may depend on p and the entire finite metric. The quantifier order is ∀p>2 ∃C_p<∞ ∀(X,d) ∃F,s; there is no single bound required to work uniformly as p varies, and p=∞ is excluded. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic running-time target.

The source writes c_Y(X,√d)≤D_p, where c_Y is the infimum of the distortions of all embeddings. The infimum need not be attained. Existence of some finite uniform bound in that formulation is equivalent to the displayed formulation: increasing an available finite infimum bound, for example to twice its value, allows actual embeddings for each finite X. The source's stronger suggestion D_p=1 instead means distortion arbitrarily close to one for every finite metric. It must not be silently replaced by a demand for an attained isometric embedding, and neither strengthening is required here.

The already-proved theorem embeds the 1/p-snowflake, with distances d(x,y)^{1/p}, with distortion arbitrarily close to one. When p>2 its exponent is smaller than 1/2, so it does not answer this question. At p=2 it does give the half-snowflake result; that endpoint is background, outside the unresolved range.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform-in-X finite-distortion assertion for every fixed p>2, or refute it by finding a fixed p>2 for which half-snowflake distortions into this exact target space are unbounded across finite metrics. A single finite metric with distortion greater than one does not refute the claim. Results allowing the distortion or base-space dimension to grow with |X|, or using exponent 1/p instead of 1/2, do not settle it. No optimal numerical value of C_p is requested.

context_blocks.title: The conjecture raises the snowflake exponent
context_blocks.text: The source proves almost-isometric universality at exponent 1/p. Question 23 of the full journal paper asks for bounded distortion at the larger exponent 1/2 when p>2. This restores the mathematical expression lost from the saved extraction.

context_blocks.title: The constant must work for every finite metric
context_blocks.text: Allowing a different, arbitrarily large distortion bound for each finite metric would remove the central uniformity requirement. The proposed C_p depends only on the fixed Wasserstein exponent.

context_blocks.title: Related questions have different demands
context_blocks.text: The source separately raises almost-isometric half-snowflake embeddings, embeddings of the entire Wasserstein-2 space into Wasserstein-p space, and sharp lower bounds above exponent 1/2. Those are not substituted for this finite-distortion conjecture.

context_blocks.text: The 2024 paper relates coarse embeddability and 1/p-snowflake universality for Wasserstein space over R² to persistence diagrams. Its stated results do not supply half-snowflake universality in R³ for p>2.

cards.context:
The source proves almost-isometric universality at exponent 1/p. Question 23 of the full journal paper asks for bounded distortion at the larger exponent 1/2 when p>2. This restores the mathematical expression lost from the saved extraction.

Allowing a different, arbitrarily large distortion bound for each finite metric would remove the central uniformity requirement. The proposed C_p depends only on the fixed Wasserstein exponent.

The source separately raises almost-isometric half-snowflake embeddings, embeddings of the entire Wasserstein-2 space into Wasserstein-p space, and sharp lower bounds above exponent 1/2. Those are not substituted for this finite-distortion conjecture.

The 2024 paper relates coarse embeddability and 1/p-snowflake universality for Wasserstein space over R² to persistence diagrams. Its stated results do not supply half-snowflake universality in R³ for p>2.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
